title: Chapter XXXIII

teacherSummary.text: Colonel Fitzwilliam mentions that Darcy recently saved a friend from an 'imprudent marriage.' Elizabeth realizes this means Jane and Bingley, and she weeps and stays home with a headache.

vocabulary.definition: Capable of being easily led, taught, or managed
vocabulary.context: I never heard any harm of her; and I dare say she is one of the most tractable creatures in the world.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tractable”: tract (Latin trahere, "to draw, pull") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: “That is not an unnatural surmise,” said Fitzwilliam, “but it is lessening the honour of my cousin’s triumph very sadly.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lessen”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Pertaining to, or being in accordance with, duty
vocabulary.context: “You are rather disposed to call his interference officious?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “officious”: fic (Latin facere, "to make") + -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: When have you been prevented by want of money from going wherever you chose, or procuring anything you had a fancy for?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “procure”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + cur (Latin cura, "care"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: That which is hard to hear, as toil, privation, injury, injustice, etc
vocabulary.context: “These are home questions—and perhaps I cannot say that I have experienced many hardships of that nature.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hardship”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn") + -ship (Old English -scipe, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The accomplishing of any purpose violently, precipitately, prematurely, or with unusual expedition
vocabulary.context: Putting away the letter immediately and forcing a smile, she said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “forcing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: One collaterally related more remotely than a brother or sister
vocabulary.context: Darcy, it determined her not to attend her cousins to Rosings, where they were engaged to drink tea.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cousin”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “Is this,” thought Elizabeth, “meant for me?” and she coloured at the idea; but, recovering herself, said in a lively tone, “And pray, what is the usual price of an Earl’s younger son?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “recover”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: To interrupt a silence which might make him fancy her affected with what had passed, she soon afterwards said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “interrupt”: inter- (Latin inter, "between") + rupt (Latin rumpere, "to break"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A speaking or notice of anything, -- usually in a brief or cursory manner
vocabulary.context: “You may depend upon my not mentioning it.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mention”: -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Interfering in a friend's courtship was seen as a sign of loyalty or arrogance, depending on view.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXIII,” how does Austen show a revelation from the colonel? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXIII develops the idea of a revelation from the colonel. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XXXIII to complicate the reader's understanding of a revelation from the colonel. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a revelation from the colonel responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a revelation from the colonel. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Fitzwilliam's casual remark hurt Elizabeth so deeply? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are tractable, lessening, officious, procuring, hardships. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I never heard any harm of her; and I dare say she is one of the most tractable creatures in the world.” Webster's says: Capable of being easily led, taught, or managed. Now the word history: “tractable”: tract (Latin trahere, "to draw, pull") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “lessen”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “officious”: fic (Latin facere, "to make") + -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Interfering in a friend's courtship was seen as a sign of loyalty or arrogance, depending on view. Why does this chapter matter? The revelation primes Elizabeth's anger for the proposal to come. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a revelation from the colonel.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Irony, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.
